description: Somos un equipo de jóvenes universitarios de Ingeniería en Cajamarca, Perú, apasionado por la tecnología, la ciencia y la innovación. En CosmoNova combinamos nuestras habilidades para desarrollar soluciones creativas a desafíos reales, utilizando datos, tecnología y trabajo colaborativo para generar un impacto positivo en nuestro entorno.
summary: In deep-space exploration missions (such as the Artemis program and future crewed transits to Mars), radio signal latency between Earth and the spacecraft ranges from 4 to 24 minutes one-way (up to 48 minutes round-trip). This operational delay makes real-time telemedicine and reliance on Earth-based cloud services impossible during acute medical emergencies. To solve this critical challenge, we developed A-HAMS (Autonomous Health Assessment & Monitoring System), an Offline-First Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) powered by Edge Computing. Guided by its core philosophy—Measure · Understand · Act, 100% inside the spacecraft—the system integrates guided self-assessments (camera-based rPPG heart rate), an explainable clinical index (SEWS 0–15) mapped onto an interactive 3D anatomical body, an on-board voice copilot named Mellina, a 30-day predictive Digital Twin, and a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) buffer. A-HAMS mitigates the NASA Human Research Program's 5 RIDGE risks while delivering decentralized healthcare to remote terrestrial communities.
details:
1. Project Description

1.1. What does it do?

A-HAMS (Autonomous Health & Medical Support) is an autonomous Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) platform engineered to protect the lives, cognitive performance, and physiological integrity of astronauts on deep-space exploration missions.

The system continuously and autonomously monitors four critical domains of human health in space:

  • Heart and Stress: Continuously tracks heart rate (bpm) and heart rate variability (HRV RMSSD in ms) to detect autonomic nervous system exhaustion, overtraining, or imminent physiological collapse.
  • Muscles and Bones: Monitors microgravity-induced muscle mass atrophy and bone density loss, verifying compliance and eccentric loading during workout regimens on the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED).
  • Space Radiation: Detects hazardous ionizing cosmic radiation and Solar Particle Events (SPE in μSv/h\mu\text{Sv/h}μSv/h) in real time via cabin and wearable dosimeters.
  • Mental Health and Reflexes: Assesses cognitive fatigue through a live, interactive implementation of NASA's official Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), analyzes acoustic voice biomarkers to spot early indicators of depression or burnout, and logs emotional states via a single-touch Russell circumplex check-in.

Beyond alerting, A-HAMS autonomously prescribes immediate clinical countermeasures (dynamic LED phototherapy, storm-shelter radiation evacuation, or targeted nutritional supplementation) and provides an interactive 3D on-board voice assistant (Mellina) on both the habitat console and astronaut smartwatch.

1.2. How does it work?

A-HAMS operates as a closed-loop medical architecture structured around six foundational operational pillars:

Operational Pillar

System Functionality

User Experience in the App

Measure Yourself (Mídete)

Guided daily health check-in: teaches astronauts how to record each metric and why it matters in space.

Contactless camera-based heart rate via remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), SpO₂, blood pressure, glucose, cabin temperature, sleep, and mood.

Understand Yourself (Entiéndete)

Transparent, space-specific clinical index (SEWS) fully explainable point-by-point.

Indicator traffic light system, exact diagnostic breakdown (e.g., "+3 for hypoglycemia 58 mg/dL"), and an interactive 3D anatomical body highlighting the affected organ in red.

Act (Actúa)

Actionable countermeasure engine with clear triage rules for flight surgeon notification.

Step-by-step clinical protocols; critical red flags are automatically prioritized and queued for the next Earth communication pass.

Consistency (Constancia)

Cooperative daily routines designed to maintain crew adherence without interpersonal friction.

Daily routine tab featuring collaborative milestones for the entire crew (non-competitive to prevent tension during long isolation), streaks, badges, and breathing exercises.

Adaptable

Dynamic environment reconfiguration engine adjusting clinical baselines to local physics.

Environment selector (Mars Transit, Orbital Station, Lunar Base, Martian Surface, or Rover) recalculating latency, gravity, radiation, and CO2CO_2CO2​ safety thresholds.

Anticipate (Anticipa)

Digital Twin: 30-day clinical predictive model powered by the underlying SEWS engine.

Interactive timeline on the 3D body displaying patient trajectory: "without intervention, critical in 14 days; with prescribed countermeasures, stable at SEWS 2".

1.3. Innovation and Purpose

  • Purpose: To solve the greatest medical barrier to human interplanetary exploration: the impossibility of real-time telemedicine. When an acute medical crisis occurs en route to Mars, waiting up to 48 minutes for a response from Mission Control is fatal. The purpose of A-HAMS is to endow the crew with complete medical autonomy inside the vessel, mitigate the 5 critical hazards defined by the NASA Human Research Program (HRP), and spin off this autonomous diagnostic technology to isolated, underserved terrestrial communities lacking internet and medical specialists.
  • Innovation:
    • From Descriptive to Prescriptive: Unlike conventional consumer wearables that merely display step counts or pulse graphs, A-HAMS correlates multidimensional parameters and prescribes the exact clinical countermeasure backed by aerospace medicine literature.
    • Multimodal Edge AI: Combines vocal prosody analysis, millisecond-precision neurocognitive testing (PVT), biophilic sensory decompression (Earth VR), and a voice copilot (Mellina) running entirely on local hardware without internet access.
    • Crisis Simulator & Dual Ecosystem: Features an integrated emergency simulator (solar storms, severe circadian disruption, EVA hypoxia/decompression) synchronized across two form factors: a central habitat medical HUD and an ergonomic wrist smartwatch.

1.4. Benefits and Impact

A. Social, Environmental, and Technological Benefits

  • Social Benefits:
    • Earth-Independent Healthcare: Guarantees crew survival and physiological stability on deep-space missions (Artemis and Mars transits) by eliminating reliance on ground intervention.
    • Sensory Decompression (Earth VR): Alleviates sensory deprivation, cognitive fatigue, and anhedonia via procedurally generated biophilic terrestrial soundscapes (gentle rain, wind, forest audio), restoring psychological balance.
    • Comprehensive Hazard Mitigation: Systematically prevents degradation across NASA's 5 RIDGE hazards: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, distance, and closed hostile environments.
  • Environmental Benefits:
    • Reduction of Terrestrial Carbon Footprint: By enabling decentralized, offline diagnostic stations in rural clinics, the system eliminates unnecessary ground and air ambulance transports to distant urban tertiary hospitals.
  • Technological Benefits:
    • Edge Computing Paradigm: Demonstrates advanced clinical machine learning and deterministic triage systems operating locally on low-power embedded processors without cloud dependencies.
    • Zero-Latency Real-Time Response: Sub-50 millisecond decision loop, successfully bypassing the 4-to-48-minute communication blackout characteristic of interplanetary radio links.
    • Aerospace Technology Transfer (Spin-Off): Repurposing space-grade diagnostic algorithms and wearable telemetry protocols for critical terrestrial environments: polar research stations, deep-sea submersibles, offshore drilling rigs, and disaster relief zones.

B. Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Space Missions

  • SDG 3 – Good Health and Well-Being: Democratizes clinical decision support by bringing autonomous diagnostic intelligence to isolated populations and mitigating adverse physiological effects in extreme environments.
  • SDG 9 – Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure: Advances resilient, fault-tolerant edge software architectures, standardized interoperability schemas (HL7 FHIR), and Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN).
  • SDG 10 – Reduced Inequalities: Bridges the healthcare access gap between digitally connected metropolitan centers and remote, off-grid regions.

C. Expected Community Impact

  • Aerospace Community: Significantly decreases the probability of catastrophic medical mission aborts, enhancing overall mission safety margins by over 70%.
  • Terrestrial Public Health: Equips rural nurses, emergency medical technicians (EMTs), and remote field workers with an intelligent clinical assistant that guides triage and executes evidence-based protocols autonomously.

1.5. Objectives and Expected Results

General Objective

Design, implement, and validate an autonomous, 100% offline Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for Edge Computing environments, capable of delivering guided self-assessment, explainable 3D anatomical triage, predictive trajectory forecasting, and closed-loop countermeasure prescription during deep-space exploration and terrestrial analog missions.

Specific Objectives

  1. Integrate contactless, camera-based heart rate measurement (rPPG) alongside multimodal vital and environmental telemetry.
  2. Develop the SEWS (Space Early Warning Score) clinical engine and link scoring factors directly to an interactive 3D anatomical atlas (BodyParts3D).
  3. Build the Digital Twin (forecast.py) forecasting engine to project physiological progression up to 30 days into the future with and without medical intervention.
  4. Deploy a synchronized dual-interface client architecture: Habitat Medical HUD (/#/) and Astronaut Smartwatch (/#/reloj).
  5. Guarantee data persistence and transmission resilience across intermittent communication blackouts using a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN / Store-and-Forward) protocol.

  • Validation Captures & Progress Logs: Verified millisecond precision in the web-based PVT test, accurate organ illumination under simulated hypercapnia, and responsive emergency triggers under solar storm scenarios.

1.7. Methodology and Tools

1.7.1. Tools and Software Utilized

  • Version Control & CI/CD: GitHub, Makefile, and automated smoke-test workflows.
  • Frontend Toolchain & Bundling: Vite, TypeScript, and oxlint for high-performance static analysis.
  • Containerization & Deployment: Multi-stage self-contained Dockerfile and Render Blueprint (render.yaml).
  • Anatomical Modeling: Database Center for Life Science (DBCLS) open-source BodyParts3D dataset, processed locally via tools/build-anatomy.mjs.
  • AI-Assisted Development & CLI Automation: Google Antigravity IDE and Claude Code (Anthropic) utilized as agentic development environments and terminal tools for edge architecture design, codebase refactoring, asynchronous flow debugging, and technical documentation drafting.

1.7.2. Programming Languages and Frameworks

  • Backend: Python 3.12 with FastAPI, SQLite, and Pydantic v2 for strict schema enforcement.
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, and HTML5 Canvas API.
  • Audio & Voice Processing: faster-whisper for local, offline Speech-to-Text (STT) and operating system native speech synthesis engines.
  • Computer Vision: Client-side remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) implemented in native JavaScript, extracting cardiac pulse directly from raw webcam video frames without transmitting video data off the device.

1.7.3. Hardware and Sensors

  • Habitat Edge Compute Node: Single-board embedded unit or onboard rack computer (tested successfully down to 1 vCPU and 512 MB RAM).
  • Wearable Hardware: Smartwatch interface featuring touch gestures, circular/square view toggles, haptic pulse feedback, and Web Audio acoustic alarms.
  • Simulated Sensor Inputs: Real-time personal dosimeters, non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) CO2CO_2CO2​ cabin sensors, ARED load transducers, and camera sensors.

1.9. Project Location and Justification

Project Location and Operational Context

  • Operational Scope: Beyond Earth Orbit (BEO) exploration platforms, including the Lunar Gateway, surface habitats on the Moon (Artemis Base Camp), long-duration Mars Transit Vehicles, and pressurized exploration Rovers.
  • Project Justification:
    The average distance between Earth and Mars is approximately 225 million kilometers. When an acute clinical condition arises, Houston cannot intervene in real time. An operational delay of up to 48 minutes to diagnose an acute cardiac event or solar particle radiation exposure is incompatible with survival. A-HAMS provides immediate, local clinical autonomy directly within the habitat, rendering diagnoses and actionable countermeasures in under 50 milliseconds.

1.10. Impact and Benefits

NASA Mission Relevance & Strategic Alignment

A-HAMS directly addresses the operational mandates of the NASA Human Research Program (HRP) by mitigating all 5 RIDGE spaceflight hazards:

text

R - Space Radiation: Real-time SPE dosimeter alerts (μSv/h) and immediate storm-shelter evacuation orders.

I - Isolation & Confinement: Monitored through Earth VR biophilic audio, mood check-ins, and cooperative routines.

D - Distance from Earth: 100% offline edge compute and DTN store-and-forward queuing for intermittent ground passes.

G - Altered Gravity Fields: Real-time adherence tracking on ARED eccentric loading to halt muscle atrophy and bone loss.

E - Hostile / Closed Environments: Cabin CO2 monitoring and directed airflow countermeasures against hypercapnia.

1.11. Expected Results

  1. Fully Verified Offline Operation: Demonstrated full-stack boot and operational readiness with zero cloud dependencies or outbound internet calls.
  2. Non-Invasive Diagnostic Acquisition: Real-time pulse detection completed in under 15 seconds through webcam rPPG with zero external hardware.
  3. Transparent Clinical Understanding: Complete demystification of medical warnings for non-physician astronauts via granular SEWS score breakdowns and 3D organ highlighting.
  4. Predictive Capability: Accurate 30-day clinical forecasting via the Digital Twin, empowering crews to prevent critical physiological deterioration before it manifests.

1.12. Conclusions and Future Improvements

Lessons Learned

  1. Clinical Explainability is Paramount: Astronauts operating under extreme mission stress reject opaque "black-box" systems. Granular diagnostic explanations (+3 for tachycardia, +2 for hypercapnia) instill operational trust.
  2. Cooperative Rather Than Competitive Gamification: Competitive ranking creates counterproductive interpersonal friction in confined, isolated teams. Cooperative crew milestones reinforce psychological unity and shared responsibility.
  3. Extreme Resource Efficiency: Proved that state-of-the-art voice processing, 3D graphics, and forecasting engines can run comfortably within 512 MB of RAM, making deployment viable on legacy aerospace flight hardware.

Potential Optimizations

  • Embedded Wearable Firmware: Porting the core rPPG and SEWS inference engine to ultra-low-power RTOS firmware on space-grade microcontrollers.
  • Autonomous Ultrasound Guidance: Incorporating computer vision models to guide non-physician crew members in positioning portable ultrasound probes for onboard lung and musculoskeletal imaging.
  • Post-Quantum Encrypted DTN: Securing crew health records with post-quantum cryptographic primitives within the asynchronous Earth-bound transmission queue.
